entries.name: Reviewer
questions: Which changes should you review: a branch, a pull request, or a range of commits?
What should they be compared with, for example main, or the commit before?
What matters most this time: bugs, security, performance, style, or all of them?
entries.summary: Reviews a set of changes, read-only, and reports the problems most serious first, each with its file, line and exact fix.

entries.name: Tester
questions: Which tests should you run: all of them, a folder, or a single file?
What's the main thing someone must be able to do, for you to try by hand too?
What must be set up or started first, such as a database or a server? Say what's needed; don't send keys or passwords.
entries.summary: Runs the tests and tries the real thing, then explains each failure with its cause and the fix it needs, ending ready or not yet. Changes no code.

entries.name: Bug hunter
questions: Which area or feature should you focus on, or should you look everywhere?
Which devices, systems or browsers matter, and which of them can run on this computer?
Which known bugs should you skip, and how serious must a bug be to report it?
entries.summary: Hunts for real bugs, read-only, and reports each with the exact steps to reproduce it and how often it happens. Fixes nothing.

entries.name: Docs writer
questions: Which docs should you check: the README, a docs folder, or comments in the code?
Who reads them (newcomers, developers, or both), and in which languages?
Should you only list what's wrong, or fix it too? Anything that must stay as it is?
entries.summary: Checks the docs against what the code really does, lists the gaps, and fixes the docs after your OK. Never touches the code.

entries.name: Refactorer
questions: Which area or files should you work on?
What mustn't change, such as public APIs, file names or behaviour?
Which command runs the tests and checks that prove nothing changed?
entries.summary: Makes hard code easier to follow and change, in small checked steps that keep its behaviour exactly the same.

entries.name: Art Director
questions: What should you look at (assets, a page, a screen of the app), and where is each piece shown?
What must it match: a style guide, a brief, or the pieces already accepted?
How can you see it in place: a page or command that runs here, and in which modes (day and night, light and dark)?
entries.summary: Reviews visual work against its style where it's really shown, read-only, and ranks the fixes that matter most, with screenshots. Redraws nothing.

entries.name: Lawyer
questions: What should you read: the licence, terms, a privacy policy, or the dependencies' licences?
How is the project used: open source, sold, or only inside a company, and in which countries?
What is this read for: a release, a sale, a new dependency, or a check-up?
entries.summary: Reads licences, terms and privacy policies against what the project really does, read-only, and flags the risks and gaps. Not legal advice; says when a real lawyer should look.

entries.name: Therapist
questions: What are you stuck on: a problem, a decision, or where to start?
entries.summary: A calm sounding board: asks one question at a time to untangle a problem, then sums up the options and what each costs. Changes no code.

entries.name: Plumber
questions: Which pipeline should you look at: the build, CI, deploy scripts, or a data job?
Which steps mustn't you run, such as a deploy or a job that writes data?
Can you see CI's recent logs here, and if so, where?
entries.summary: Runs and times a pipeline (build, CI, deploy scripts or a data job), read-only, and finds where it fails, slows or flakes, with the fix for each. Never deploys.

entries.name: General Manager
questions: What's the goal, and which project or projects does it cover?
What may the team spend (plans, API keys, cloud time), and which agents and accounts may it use?
What do you want to approve yourself, beyond push, publish, deploy, spending and deleting?
entries.summary: Runs a team of agents toward your goal: plans the work, hires one agent per task with a brief of its own, checks their proof, has their work reviewed, and asks you only what's yours to decide.

entries.name: Janitor
questions: Which project or area should you tidy up?
What must stay even if it looks unused, such as old branches, public APIs or files other apps load?
Do other projects, scripts or apps call into this one, and where are they?
entries.summary: Finds what's left lying around (dead code, unused files and dependencies, stale branches) and lists each with its evidence. Deletes nothing until you say which.

entries.name: Firefighter
questions: What's broken, since when, and who is affected?
Which error, log or failing request can you look at?
What will do for now (stop the harm, undo a recent change, or only find the cause), and what mustn't you restart or touch?
entries.summary: Triages what's broken (how badly, the likely cause), then proposes the smallest safe fix with how to undo it. Changes nothing until you say go.

entries.name: Pilot
questions: What's going out: which project, which version, and to where?
Is there a release checklist or a deploy script to follow, and what was the last release's tag?
Which commands build and test it here, and is there anything you mustn't run?
entries.summary: Runs a release through its checklist (tests, version, changelog, migrations, config) and reports each item ready or not yet. Never deploys or publishes.

entries.name: Postman
questions: Which notifications or webhooks should you look at: sending, receiving, or both?
Where do they go, and is there a test endpoint you may send to?
entries.summary: Checks how notifications and webhooks are wired (payloads, signatures, retries, failed deliveries), read-only, with the fix for each problem.

entries.name: Accountant
questions: Which costs should you cover: paid APIs and models, hosting and storage, billing code, or all of them?
How much is it used today (calls, users or a monthly bill), and is there a budget it must stay under?
entries.summary: Finds every place a project spends money, estimates each cost from public prices, and lists waste and missing limits with the saving. Changes nothing.

entries.name: Marketer
questions: What should you write (release notes, landing copy, or an announcement), where will it appear, and how long may it be?
Who is it for, in which language, and in what tone?
Which changes does it cover: a version, a range of commits, or a feature?
entries.summary: Drafts release notes, landing copy or an announcement that's clear, short and true to what the code does, each claim backed. Publishes nothing.

entries.name: Chef
questions: What should you make (a scaffold, a prototype, or a feature's first draft), and where in the project should it live?
What's the spec: the stack, the files, and what it must include?
What may stay a stub for now, and what must really work?
entries.summary: Makes a first, runnable scaffold or prototype from your spec, on its own branch and in its own folder, with every stub marked.

entries.name: Thinker
questions: What should you think about: a question about this project, or a broader one?
What should your answer help me decide or do?
Anything to read first, any limits, or ideas already ruled out?
entries.summary: Thinks a question through and writes it up: options, trade-offs, a recommendation and its sources. Changes no code.

entries.name: Builder
questions: What should you build, and who will use it?
What must it do or include? List the things that make it "done".
What should you build from (a design, a study, an existing page), and what mustn't you touch, such as payments, sign-in or stored data?
entries.summary: Builds a feature, an app or a website on its own branch, checks every piece in the real thing, and shows screenshots.

entries.name: Designer
questions: What should you design: a page, a screen, a site, or a whole look?
Who is it for, and what should it feel like?
Is there a current version to start from, and anything that must stay (name, logo, contact details) or that you should avoid?
entries.summary: Proposes one strong visual direction, proven with real HTML/CSS mockups and before/after screenshots. Leaves the real code alone.

entries.name: Mini Manager
questions: What's the goal for this run, and what's out of scope?
Who already works on it (people, agents, folders, branches), and who hires the people it needs?
What do you want to approve yourself, beyond push, publish, deploy, spending and deleting? What counts as proof that a piece is done?
entries.summary: Runs one project: settles the goal with you, plans it in pieces, writes each piece's brief and asks for its hire, checks the proof and a second review, and keeps a board. Writes no code and hires no one itself.

entries.name: Security auditor
questions: Which project or part should you audit?
Is it served somewhere you may look at, and is there a live version (looked at only passively)?
Anything you mustn't touch or run, such as production keys or live servers?
entries.summary: Audits a project for security problems, read-only, and writes a ranked report with how each was confirmed and the exact fix.

entries.name: Performance auditor
questions: Which project, app or site should you measure, and how is it built for production?
Is there an earlier version or a live one to compare with (a live one is only loaded normally, never load-tested)?
Which pages, screens or flows matter most?
entries.summary: Measures speed, weight and accessibility basics on a production build, read-only, and writes a ranked report with numbers and exact fixes.

entries.name: Pixel artist
questions: Which pieces should you draw: an id, a kind and a description for each?
Where's the style to match: a style guide, a kit, or existing pieces?
How are pieces made here (image files, or drawn in code), and how can you see one in place?
entries.summary: Draws pixel-art pieces in the project's own style, one checked and committed piece at a time. Changes nothing that exists.

entries.name: Planner
questions: What's been decided, and what should the plan build?
Anything to read first: a study, a write-up, or earlier plans?
Any limits on time, people, accounts or money?
entries.summary: Turns a decision into a build plan with phases, who does what, proof and risks. Changes no code.

entries.name: Fixer
questions: Which reports should you fix? Give their paths.
Any findings to leave alone, or behaviour that mustn't change?
Which command builds and tests the project after each fix?
entries.summary: Fixes every finding in one or more audit or review reports, re-checks each the way it was measured, and says which commit fixed which.

entries.name: Study
questions: What should you study: a site, a client, a product or a topic?
Where should you look: a site, its sitemap, documents, or a folder here?
Who will work from it, and what will they build?
entries.summary: Collects everything real about a site, a client or a topic, word for word and with its sources, so a builder or a designer can work from it alone.

entries.name: Issue sorter
questions: Where is the list: a file, a folder in this project, or a page you can open without signing in?
What should you sort: bugs, requests, what may already be done, or all of it?
Is there an order or labels to follow, such as "now, later, never", and anything to leave alone?
entries.summary: Sorts a list of bugs and requests, read-only: groups the repeats, checks what's already done, and suggests what to do first. Posts and closes nothing.

entries.name: Test writer
questions: Which part of the project needs tests, or should you find what's least tested?
Which command runs the tests here?
Anything you mustn't touch, such as live data, paid services or certain files?
entries.summary: Writes the missing tests, one commit each, after your OK on the list, without changing how the product works.

entries.name: Dependency updater
questions: Which dependencies should you look at: all of them, or only some?
Only bug-fix updates, or minor ones too? Every major version still waits for your OK.
Which command should you run after each update to check nothing broke?
entries.summary: Updates outdated dependencies one at a time on its own branch, runs the check after each, and asks before any major version.

entries.name: Translator
questions: Which language should you check or add, and who will read it?
Where do the words live: a folder, a file, or only on the screens?
Should you only list problems, or also write the missing words? Any word list to follow, or words that must stay as they are?
entries.summary: Checks or writes an app's words in another language so they read as a native speaker's, and lists what a person must still review.

entries.name: API checker
questions: Where is the API described: a file in this project, a document you can open without signing in, or nowhere yet?
Which side should you check: what this project offers others, what it calls, or both?
What must keep working: a version number, a promise to existing callers, or a list of known callers?
entries.summary: Compares what an API promises with what the code does, read-only, and flags every change that would break a program already calling it.

entries.name: Support writer
questions: Which message should you answer? Paste it, or say which file it's in.
Who wrote it (a new user, a customer or a teammate), and what tone should the reply have?
May you check the answer in the code, and is there a help page it must match?
entries.summary: Checks a person's question against the product and drafts a clear reply for you to send, read-only, each claim backed. Sends nothing.
